sysd-scale-026.title: Spanner: a SQL database spread across the globe
sysd-scale-026.text:
Spanner gives Google a SQL database spread across the globe that still answers with strong consistency. It is a scalable, multiversion, globally distributed and synchronously replicated SQL database, with automatic multi-site replication and failover. Its authors describe it as the first system to distribute data at global scale and support externally-consistent distributed transactions. Users can run arbitrary SQL queries on relational data, and transactions can span rows, columns, tables and databases within one Spanner universe. Data is versioned, so clients can read previous versions, subject to garbage collection windows.

Underneath, Spanner uses the Paxos algorithm to shard data across up to hundreds of servers, spread over many Paxos state machines. The unusual ingredient is time. It leans on hardware-assisted clock synchronization with GPS and atomic clocks, and its TrueTime service gives monotonically increasing timestamps in data centers worldwide. The paper's time API exposes clock uncertainty, which is critical to external consistency, nonblocking reads in the past, lock-free snapshot transactions and atomic schema changes.

sysd-scale-042.title: Amazon Dynamo: a key-value store built for constant failure
sysd-scale-042.text:
On a platform that runs on tens of thousands of servers and network components in many datacenters around the world, something is always failing. Reliability at that scale is one of Amazon's biggest challenges, because even the slightest outage has significant financial consequences and impacts customer trust. How persistent state is managed in the face of these failures drives the reliability and scalability of the software.

Many Amazon services mostly read data by primary key and put speed first, and joining the pieces of data that traditional databases split apart was extremely taxing. Amazon's response was Dynamo, a highly available key-value store built for internal use, which accepted a compromise in storage efficiency. Adoption lagged, because engineers avoided the overhead of provisioning and managing partitions and nodes; the later service in {{ref:sysd-scale-027}} automated those operations. Cassandra incorporates Dynamo's distributed storage and replication techniques.

sysd-scale-027.title: Amazon DynamoDB: Dynamo as a managed service
sysd-scale-027.text:
Engineers at Amazon avoided Dynamo because running it meant provisioning and managing partitions and nodes. DynamoDB, a managed NoSQL database service from AWS, automated those operations. It supports key-value and document data. DynamoDB hashes the partition key to pick a partition. Each partition stores up to 10 GB and by default handles 1,000 write capacity units and 3,000 read capacity units. One read capacity unit is one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to 4 KB. One write capacity unit is one write per second for an item up to 1 KB.

Each partition has three nodes holding copies, with one leader chosen by Paxos. The leader sends a heartbeat every 1.5 seconds, and a node that stops hearing it can start a new election. A write goes to the leader, then a second node, then returns success while propagation continues to the third. A consistent read visits the leader, while an eventually consistent read picks a random node, trading consistency for availability so reads do not overload one node.

sysd-scale-028.title: DynamoDB partition and sort keys: choosing where items live
sysd-scale-028.text: Every DynamoDB table needs a primary key, one or two attributes that uniquely identify each item and decide where it is stored. A key of one attribute is a partition key, which determines the physical location of the item. A key of two attributes is a partition key plus a sort key. The partition key picks the location and the sort key orders items inside it; items may share a partition key but not a sort key. A local secondary index keeps the table's partition key with a different sort key, while a global secondary index uses a different partition key.

sysd-scale-029.title: DynamoDB data modeling patterns: laying data out for access
sysd-scale-029.text: In DynamoDB the layout of the data follows the questions it will be asked. Data modeling patterns are ways to lay data out, chosen to match a workload's access patterns. Single Table Design keeps related data together under one partition key, within the 400KB item size limit, to cut access latency. Multiple Table Design isolates data into purpose-specific tables by access pattern, and Hybrid Design blends the two. A layout that stores data changes as immutable events lets past state be rebuilt; see {{ref:sysd-msg-021}}. Materialized Views pre-aggregate data. Time-Series Design suits logging and metrics: the partition key identifies the entity and the sort key holds the timestamp.

sysd-scale-025.title: Google File System: reliable storage on cheap, failing machines
sysd-scale-025.text:
Google's search engine generates enormous amounts of data that must be retained, and Google chose to keep it on clusters of cheap commodity computers. The Google File System was built for that job: a proprietary distributed file system that gives efficient, reliable access to data on large clusters of commodity hardware. Cheap machines fail often, so the design must guard against the high failure rate of individual nodes and the data loss that follows. Its other decisions favor high data throughput, even when that costs latency.

Files are split into fixed-size chunks of 64 megabytes. They are usually appended to or read, and only extremely rarely overwritten or shrunk. A cluster has one master node and many chunkservers. The master gives each chunk a globally unique 64-bit label when it creates it and keeps the mapping from files to chunks. It stores metadata rather than chunks, including where each chunk's copies live, and stays current through periodic heartbeat messages from every chunkserver. Each chunk is replicated across the network, three times by default but configurable, and files in high demand may get a higher replication factor.

A read shows why this scales. A client asks the master where a chunk lives, then reads the data directly from a chunkserver, so the master stays out of the data path. Because the master is not involved in reads, read rate grows with the number of chunkservers, reaching 583 MB/s for 342 nodes.

Writes are controlled by time-limited leases. The master lets one process modify a chunk for a finite period, and no other process gets permission during it. The primary chunk holder pushes each change to the other chunkservers holding copies. The change is not saved until all of them acknowledge, which makes the operation atomic. Record Append lets many clients append to the same file at once, with atomicity guaranteed. GFS does not provide a POSIX interface. The lesson in the numbers: the master holds only metadata and stays off the data path, so adding chunkservers adds read capacity.

sysd-scale-038.title: Bigtable: Google's structured storage at petabyte scale
sysd-scale-038.text:
As of April 2024, Bigtable manages over 10 Exabytes of data and serves more than 7 billion requests per second. It is a distributed storage system for structured data, designed to scale to petabytes across thousands of commodity servers. Many Google projects store data in it, such as web indexing, Google Earth and Google Finance. Their demands run from URLs to satellite imagery in size and from bulk processing to real-time serving in latency. Google built its own database for scalability and better control of performance.

Bigtable is built on Colossus, the Google File System, together with the Chubby lock service and SSTable log-structured storage. Tables are split into tablets of a few hundred megabytes or a few gigabytes, and hundreds to thousands of servers serve thousands to hundreds of thousands of tablets. Tablet locations live in META1 tablets, found via the single META0 tablet, which is not a bottleneck because lookups are cheap and clients aggressively cache locations. HBase and Cassandra are the best-known open source projects modeled after it.

sysd-scale-031.title: Apache Cassandra: a database with no special node
sysd-scale-031.text:
Cassandra has no head node. All nodes perform identical functions, so there is no single point of failure. It is an open-source distributed database that handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers. It was designed to run on cheap commodity hardware and to handle high write throughput without sacrificing read efficiency. It aims to run on hundreds of nodes, possibly across data centers, where components fail continuously. The recipe combines Amazon's Dynamo storage and replication techniques with Google's Bigtable data storage engine model.

Replication is asynchronous and masterless, and a cluster can span multiple data centers. Cassandra scales linearly: adding nodes raises read and write throughput while service continues. It is classed as an AP system, favoring availability and partition tolerance over consistency. Consistency levels are tunable for reads and writes, though strict consistency suits it poorly. It offers a simple wide-column model rather than a full relational one and suits well-defined access patterns that can be built into the schema. It has no multi-table JOINs, ad hoc aggregations or complex queries.

sysd-scale-040.title: MapReduce: two functions and a cluster that does the rest
sysd-scale-040.text:
A large server farm can use MapReduce to sort a petabyte of data in only a few hours. It is a programming model and implementation for processing large data sets on a cluster. The user writes a map function, which filters and sorts, and a reduce function, which summarizes. The runtime parallelizes the work across the cluster, handles machine failures and schedules communication. The paper's key contribution is not the two functions but the scalability and resilience to failure they bring a variety of applications.

In the map step each worker applies the function to its local data. Shuffle redistributes data by output key so one key's data sits on one worker, and reduce processes each key's group in parallel. If a node falls silent, the master marks it dead and gives its work to other nodes. The paper reports more than ten thousand distinct programs at Google over four years. There are limits: it is usually not effective for quick jobs whose data fits in one machine's memory, and iterative algorithms such as graph processing are difficult.

sysd-scale-035.title: Apache Hadoop: shipping the code to the data
sysd-scale-035.text:
Hadoop's central trick is to ship the program to the data instead of the data to the program. It is a collection of open-source software utilities for reliable, scalable, distributed computing, built around HDFS storage and MapReduce processing. Both were inspired by Google's papers on MapReduce and the Google File System. Hadoop splits files into large blocks spread across the cluster. It then sends packaged code to the nodes so they process in parallel the data they hold, which is data locality. That lets a dataset be processed faster than on a conventional supercomputer architecture that moves data over high-speed networking.

The base framework has Hadoop Common, HDFS, YARN (introduced in 2012) for cluster resources and scheduling, and MapReduce. Hadoop 3 allows multiple name nodes, which removes the single point of failure of Hadoop 2's one namenode, and uses erasure coding to decrease storage overhead. Hadoop suits batch-oriented, very data-intensive work; it is not for real-time work. Yahoo's Search Webmap, running on a Linux cluster of more than 10,000 cores, produced data used in every Yahoo web search query.

sysd-scale-036.title: HDFS architecture: one NameNode, many DataNodes
sysd-scale-036.text:
HDFS declares a storage machine dead after 2 minutes of silence, then starts copying its blocks elsewhere. It is Hadoop's distributed, scalable file system, storing large files across many machines. One NameNode tracks the files and holds the metadata, such as the number of blocks, which DataNodes store them and where replicas live. DataNodes store the blocks, and each sends a heartbeat to the NameNode every 3 seconds. Reliability comes from replicating data across hosts. With the default replication value of 3, two copies sit on one rack and one on a different rack. That keeps data available if a rack loses power or a switch fails.

The secondary namenode is not a standby for failover: it checkpoints the primary's directory information so a failed primary can restart without replaying the whole journal. The single NameNode can become a bottleneck with many small files, and HDFS Federation allows multiple namespaces served by separate namenodes. HDFS gives up full POSIX compliance for higher data throughput, and it suits mostly immutable files rather than concurrent writes.

sysd-scale-120.title: Apache HBase: Bigtable on top of Hadoop
sysd-scale-120.text: Google's Bigtable has an open-source cousin that runs on Hadoop. HBase is a non-relational distributed database modeled after Bigtable and written in Java. It runs on top of HDFS, a fault-tolerant way to store large quantities of sparse data with fast reads and writes at high throughput. It is a wide-column store with compression, in-memory operation and Bloom filters per column. It is not a direct replacement for a classic SQL database and has no SQL of its own, though Apache Phoenix adds a SQL layer. In CAP terms HBase is a CP system, and like Bigtable it is rated PC/EC under PACELC.

sysd-scale-032.title: The Cassandra data model: keyspaces, tables and partition keys
sysd-scale-032.text: A Cassandra table is not as rigid as a relational one: rows in the same table can have different columns. Data is organized as keyspace, table, then row. A keyspace is like a database and sets the replication strategy. Each row is identified by a primary key whose first component is the partition key, and rows within a partition are clustered by the remaining key columns. Tables can be created, dropped or altered at run-time without blocking updates and queries. Each column carries timestamp metadata used to resolve write conflicts by last write wins, and the model is denormalized rather than joined.

sysd-scale-034.title: Cassandra gossip and failure handling: every node judges its peers
sysd-scale-034.text: No node in a Cassandra cluster is in charge of knowing who is alive. Nodes routinely gossip cluster state, such as node bootstrap times and logical clock values, and use the clock values to ignore outdated state. A few seed nodes are guaranteed gossip contact points, which removes single points of failure. Each node judges the availability of the others with the Phi Accrual Failure Detector. A node that fails to respond is convicted and removed from writes, but can rejoin when heartbeats resume. With hinted handoff, the coordinator stores a write meant for an offline node as a hint and forwards it when the node returns.

sysd-scale-033.title: Cassandra's write and read path: commit log, Memtable, SSTable
sysd-scale-033.text: Cassandra never overwrites data in place. It uses a log-structured merge tree index to optimize write throughput, unlike the B-tree indexes most databases use. A write goes to the commit log, a write-ahead log that ensures durability, and to the Memtable, an in-memory structure sorted by primary key. When the Memtable reaches size or time thresholds it flushes to an SSTable, an immutable file. Reads check the Memtable, then search SSTables from newest to oldest using bloom filters. Every change adds a new entry, and deletes use tombstones, which can slow delete-heavy workloads. Compaction merges SSTables to cut storage, drop tombstoned rows and speed reads.

sysd-scale-121.title: ScyllaDB: a Cassandra-compatible rewrite in C++
sysd-scale-121.text: ScyllaDB's authors claim up to 2 million requests per second on one machine, and a cluster that matches a Cassandra cluster 10 times its size. Independent tests sometimes measured only about 2x. It is a source-available distributed wide-column data store designed to be compatible with Apache Cassandra, with significantly higher throughput and lower latency. It speaks Cassandra's CQL protocol and the DynamoDB API, but it is a complete rewrite in C++20 on the Seastar asynchronous library. Each node is sharded per CPU core: cores share nothing and communicate explicitly. Like Cassandra it is an AP database, with Paxos for lightweight transactions and Raft for schema and topology changes.

sysd-scale-039.title: The Bigtable data model: a sorted map with timestamps
sysd-scale-039.text: Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, multi-dimensional sorted map. It maps two arbitrary strings, a row key and a column key, plus a timestamp, to an arbitrary byte array. It is not a relational database but a prototypical wide-column store, and it gives clients dynamic control over data layout and format. Each cell can hold zero or more timestamped versions of its data, and the timestamps allow both versioning and garbage collection of expired data. Google's copy of the web fits in one table. The row key is a domain-reversed URL, columns describe page properties, and the page column keeps versions stamped by fetch time.

sysd-scale-037.title: Hadoop job scheduling and YARN: from JobTracker to resource manager
sysd-scale-037.text: In first-generation Hadoop, one JobTracker handed out all the MapReduce work. It pushes work to available TaskTracker nodes, keeping work as close to the data as possible. With a rack-aware file system, work that cannot run on the node holding the data goes to a node in the same rack. That reduces traffic on the main backbone network. By default Hadoop schedules by FIFO with 5 priorities. The fair scheduler gives pools a guaranteed minimum share, and the capacity scheduler gives queues a fraction of total capacity. YARN, the biggest change in Hadoop 2, replaced this engine with a resource manager and a master for each application.

sysd-scale-041.title: MapReduce dataflow: from input splits to the shuffle
sysd-scale-041.text: The shuffle in a MapReduce job can take longer than the computation it feeds. A job flows through an input reader, map, partition, shuffle, sort, reduce and output writer. The input reader cuts input from stable storage into splits of 64 MB to 128 MB, one per Map call. A partition function sends each map output to a reducer, typically by hashing the key modulo the number of reducers. It should spread data roughly uniformly, or the job waits on slow reducers. A Combiner function can shrink the data sent over the network. In word count, map emits each word with a count and reduce sums them.

sysd-scale-030.title: Discord message storage: from MongoDB to Cassandra to ScyllaDB
sysd-scale-030.text:
Discord's first version stored messages on a single MongoDB replica, and the story since is one of outgrowing each system in turn. Around November 2015 MongoDB held 100 million messages. RAM could no longer hold the data and index, latency became unpredictable, and storage had to move. Discord chose Cassandra. In 2017 it ran 12 Cassandra nodes with billions of messages; at the start of 2022 it ran 177 nodes with trillions.

By then Cassandra had become a burden. Its latency was unpredictable, and maintenance operations had become too expensive to run. Cassandra's LSM tree makes reads more expensive than writes, and many concurrent reads on a server with hundreds of users create hotspots. Cluster maintenance such as compacting SSTables hurts performance, and garbage collection pauses cause significant latency spikes.

The answer was ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database written in C++. Discord redesigned its architecture around a monolithic API, a data service written in Rust, and ScyllaDB-based storage. The payoff shows in the tail. The p99 read latency is 15ms on ScyllaDB against 40-125ms on Cassandra, and the p99 write latency is 5ms against 5-70ms. The thread through the story is predictability: each system was left when its latency stopped being predictable.

openers.how-the-big-distributed-data-systems-wor: Google built a distributed file system for large clusters of commodity hardware, a storage system for structured data across thousands of commodity servers, and a SQL database that is synchronously replicated around the world. Amazon built a highly available key-value store to keep persistent state reliable while components fail all the time, and AWS now sells a managed NoSQL service. Open-source projects followed: Cassandra, which handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers with no single point of failure, and Hadoop and HBase, built around HDFS or modeled after Google's storage system. This chapter opens each of them up. Each one is an answer to the same question: how do you keep working when machines fail?

reviews.how-the-big-distributed-data-systems-wor: These systems rest on a few shared ideas applied to different jobs. Spanner stays strongly consistent through synchronous replication, DynamoDB lets a read trade consistency for availability, and Cassandra favors availability with tunable consistency. The Google File System, Bigtable, HDFS and HBase split data into chunks, tablets or blocks spread across commodity machines, with a master or NameNode holding metadata and heartbeats exposing dead nodes. Cassandra's write path, Bigtable's data model and MapReduce's shuffle show how each design pays for its strengths with a limit elsewhere. Discord's move from MongoDB to Cassandra and then to ScyllaDB shows what happens when a design meets a real workload.
